The app also logs “failed rides” and can auto‑file a complaint to the provider. | | **WHO PAYS** | Urban commuters (18‑35 y) who use ride‑hailing at least 2 × week and are willing to pay for a “no‑surprise” experience. | | **PRICE** | ₦500 / month subscription (≈ $1) for unlimited price‑compare + reliability score. A free tier shows only the cheapest price (no reliability data). | | **EXISTING COMPETITORS** | • Uber & Bolt apps (no cross‑provider comparison)
• “Bolt‑price‑compare” Chrome extensions (very niche, not mobile)
• Local “price‑watch” Telegram channels (manual, no API) | | **MONETIZATION FIT** | Nigerian riders are price‑sensitive **but** a small monthly fee for guaranteed reliability is attractive when they have repeatedly lost money/time. However, conversion from free to paid is historically low (< 5 %). | | **FIRST WEEK** | 1️⃣ Scrape publicly documented price‑estimate endpoints for Uber & Bolt (they already exist for “fare‑estimate”).
2️⃣ Build a simple Android UI that shows the two quotes side‑by‑side.
3️⃣ Launch a closed‑beta on the university’s WhatsApp group, collect screenshots & acceptance‑rate data for the first 50 rides. | | **WHY NOW** | The Play‑Store reviews show a *spike* in dissatisfaction (multiple recent 1‑star complaints). The core idea is to craft the input prompt so that the first output token answers the question. This makes it possible to get a decision with a single forward pass.

Find duplicate code blocks meaningful to the language (classes/functions), not just lines.

Find near-duplicates: ignore whitespace, strings, high level AST nodes such as function and names.

Find structurally similar code: anonymize identifiers, constants, etc.
